🩹 “Non-Combat Sprained Democracy”: How to Hide a Losing War

The Iran war is going so well that Central Command has quietly stopped telling Americans when their own troops are getting hit. 

Instead, injuries disappear into aggregate spreadsheets and euphemisms about “operational security,” while officials swear everything is fine and accuse critics of “fabrications.” 

Meanwhile, two more soldiers are dead in Jordan, one is missing, helicopters are damaged, and more than 400 U.S. service members have been injured since the conflict began — numbers that only leak out in fragments and delays.

If a soldier is hurt and “quickly returns to duty,” it doesn’t count for the public. If several bases are hit in a week, that becomes a line about “responding to attacks on commercial shipping,” as if the war is happening to cargo, not to very real people in uniform. 

The casualty database is “regularly updated,” we are told — but it only shows totals, not specific mass‑casualty incidents, and even the death count lags behind reality. 

When journalists and families notice the gaps, the Pentagon says critics are cherry‑picking numbers “without context.” Translation: trust the people who already misled you.

This is what losing looks like in a highly‑managed democracy. The war has drained high‑end munitions, exposed that Iran’s missile arsenal is battered but very much alive, and still Washington can’t clearly explain what “victory” even means. 

The White House repeats “never allowing Iran to have a nuclear weapon” like a magic spell, while Tehran keeps firing missiles and drones at U.S. positions and surviving repeated strikes. 

Every new attack that kills or injures Americans is sold as a reason to “stiffen resolve,” not to question the premise.

The cruelty is that the opacity isn’t just aimed at Iran — it’s aimed at American citizens. By hiding the real scale and pattern of injuries, the Pentagon keeps Congress, the press, and the public from seeing how often bases are hit, how exposed troops are, and how thin the margin of “control” has become. 

Casualty transparency — the bare minimum in a republic that claims to honor its soldiers — turns into a bargaining chip in the PR battle. The message to service members is clear: your deaths will be honored; your injuries are a data‑management issue.

And while officials sanitize the numbers, the war still kills over a thousand Iranian civilians and keeps pushing the region toward deeper chaos. But that, too, is wrapped in jargon: “sites,” “targets,” “capabilities.” 

The war is sold as a clean, precision exercise; the mess gets pushed offstage. The U.S. isn’t just de‑risking its empire — it’s de‑risking the truth.

The question practically asks itself: if the mission were working, would they really need to lie by omission about how many Americans are getting hurt?

🔔 Bitcoin price nears Fidelity’s power law support: Accumulation zone or missing catalyst? 

📌 On his power law model, a logarithmic chart that bounds Bitcoin’s entire price history between an upper resistance curve, a middle trendline, and a lower support curve, the floor currently sits near 58,000 dollars. That lower line has caught every major Bitcoin bottom since 2015. Timmer’s label for the zone the market has now entered is unambiguous: accumulation. His caveat is just as unambiguous: he sees no catalyst for a reversal, and he is not calling a bottom.

⚠️ That combination, a historically reliable floor approaching and a strategist refusing to ring the bell, is the most honest summary of the Bitcoin market in July 2026. The asset is coming off its worst quarter since the 2022 bear market, spot ETFs just recorded their largest quarterly outflow since launch, the speculative premium that carried the price past 120,000 dollars last year has evaporated, and the fast money has visibly rotated elsewhere, first into gold, then into semiconductor stocks. And yet the two quantitative measures Timmer trusts most, the deviation from the power law trendline and the Bitcoin-to-gold ratio, have both sunk to depths recorded at exactly two prior moments: the 2018 low and the 2022 low. Both of those moments were generational buying opportunities. Both also felt like the end of the world at the time.

🔖 This feature takes the model seriously in both directions: what the power law actually says, why its track record earns attention, and why the missing-catalyst objection is not a hedge but the core of the analysis.

⚡️ Guardian Council spokesperson: Iran’s enemies committed to no human rights principles

📌 Sari, IRNA – Iran’s enemies have shown that they are committed to no principles or rules of human rights, the spokesperson for the Guardian Council says.

Speaking at a gathering of Guardian Council observers in Amol, northern Iran, on Monday, Hadi Tahan Nazif said Iran should not become preoccupied with internal issues and lose sight of its adversaries as it is currently engaged in an existential and identity-based confrontation with global hegemonic powers.
​
“Today, the enemy has shown that it is committed to no principles or rules of human rights,” he said.
​
Tahan Nazif said international humanitarian law establishes rules that must be observed during armed conflicts, but the United States and Israel have violated such principles by bombing a school in Minab, a hospital in Ahvaz and other public places.
​
He said the confrontation between Iran and global hegemonic powers was rooted in fundamental differences over the principles of the Islamic Republic, adding that Iran’s Constitution emphasizes human dignity, independence, freedom and justice.
​
The official also called for unity, citing Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Sayyid Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei as stressing that division and disputes weaken a nation and undermine its power.
